chapter: Coleman Hawkins, Bernie Young and doubling on tenor
title: Frankie Trumbauer, C-melody and keeping one's own style
summary: He remarks on the C-melody saxophone, Trumbauer's advice to stay on tenor and Hawkins praising his independence from others' influence.

story.theme_name: The reed and horn player's craft: clarinet, sax, tone
story.community_name: Coleman Hawkins and the great saxophonists

blocks.x: Well, why did that instrument get dropped? Because that had a certain -- I mean like what was that, Frankie Trumbauer (unintelligible).
Now, I mean he did things on there which were very individual.

I was good friends. He used to tell me, said, you were on alto, said, why did you go back to tenor? I said, I like the tenor better. He said, stay on it. And Hawk always told me, he says, look, says, you got -- one thing about it I like about you. You don't let nobody influence you. He said, you got your own way of doing things. I said, well, Hawk, I learned that. Just part of me, I said, I love everybody's playing, but I won't let their influence just -- like in later years in New York when bebop came in, once you hear one wind instrument playing a solo, you almost hear all the other instruments because everybody's (unintelligible). But --
